u001.text: The kind of machine that answers your questions weighs more than a tonne and draws as much power as a hundred homes.

u002.text: Ask it why your cat sounds like a carburettor, and watch what that monster does. A few words. A pause. A few more words.

u003.text: It is the most powerful computer most of us will ever touch, and yet it writes like someone pecking at a keyboard.

u005.text: The obvious guess is that it is thinking hard, that every single word takes a staggering amount of maths.

u006.text: Keep that guess in mind, because we are going to test it. The real answer explains nearly everything about the buildings behind artificial intelligence.

u007.text: To see it, let's follow a single word of your question on its trip. The word cat.

u008.text: Cat leaves your phone as a radio wave and reaches a mast down the street.

u009.text: From there it travels as light, trapped inside a strand of glass thinner than a hair.

u010.text: But how do you keep light inside a bent piece of glass?

u011.text: In eighteen forty two, a Swiss physicist called Daniel Colladon showed the trick with a jet of water.

u012.text: Light that hits the inside of the jet at a shallow angle cannot escape, so it follows the water as it curves.

u013.text: Glass fibre does exactly the same thing, bouncing the light off its walls over and over.

u014.text: In twenty seventeen, a team at Heriot Watt University in Edinburgh actually filmed it.

u015.text: Their camera caught a pulse of light racing around a coil of fibre, loop after loop.

u016.text: In glass, light covers about two hundred thousand kilometres every second.

u017.text: A thousand kilometres of cable costs cat about five thousandths of a second.

u018.text: So the trip is not the slow part. Hold on to that.

u019.text: The light ends in a warehouse of computers, like the one built for OpenAI in Abilene, Texas.

u020.text: And there cat runs into its first problem. The chips inside cannot read.

u021.text: They only understand numbers, so your question has to be chopped into pieces first.

u022.text: The way it gets chopped comes from an unlikely place.

u023.text: In February nineteen ninety four, a programmer in Colorado Springs called Philip Gage wrote a magazine article about shrinking files.

u024.text: His idea was simple. Find the pair of characters that appears most often, and replace it with a new symbol.

u025.text: Then do it again, and again, until the file is small.

u026.text: Two decades later, Rico Sennrich and his colleagues borrowed that trick to split words for translation software.

u027.text: Common words end up as single pieces, rare ones as fragments, and every piece gets a number.

u028.text: ChatGPT's tokenizer works the same way. In it, cat with a space in front is number nine thousand and fifty nine.

u029.text: That number is a key. It unlocks a long list of other numbers, a kind of address for the meaning of the word.

u030.text: On a map, two numbers say where something is.

u031.text: Here every token gets thousands of them, so it sits somewhere in a space with thousands of directions.

u032.text: Training arranges that space so that cat ends up near dog, and a long way from carburettor.

u033.text: But cat is not done yet. Now comes the climb.

u034.text: OpenAI does not say how big the models behind ChatGPT are.

u035.text: But in twenty twenty five it published an open model built the same way, with the blueprint.

u036.text: That model is made of about a hundred and seventeen billion numbers, called weights.

u037.text: Nobody typed them in. Training tuned them, step by step, on trillions of tokens of text.

u038.text: They are stacked in thirty six layers, like the floors of a tower, and cat has to climb every floor.

u039.text: On each floor, cat looks back at every word before it and decides which ones matter. That step is called attention.

u040.text: It is how the word it gets linked to the thing it refers to.

u041.text: Then cat visits a crowd of smaller networks on that floor, called experts.

u042.text: But it does not visit all of them. A small router sends it to just four out of a hundred and twenty eight.

u043.text: So on the whole climb, cat only touches about five billion weights.

u044.text: Each touch is a multiplication and an addition, so that is roughly ten billion operations for a single new word.

u045.text: What comes out of the top floor is not a sentence. It is a score for every possible next piece.

u046.text: The system picks one, usually a likely one, with a little randomness so it does not sound like a robot.

u047.text: And then the whole climb starts again from the ground floor, for the next piece.

u048.text: A long answer means hundreds of climbs, one after another.

u049.text: Ten billion operations for every word. So that must be the stutter, right? The maths?

u050.text: Actually, no. That guess is wrong. The arithmetic is the easy part.

u051.text: To see what the real problem is, picture the chip as a factory.

u052.text: The workers who do the multiplying sit at desks. The weights do not live with them.

u053.text: They live in a warehouse next door, and for every new piece of the answer, they have to be trucked in.

u054.text: All of the weights that cat touches, every time. For that open model, the load is about five gigabytes.

u055.text: Now take a Blackwell chip from NVIDIA, the kind in that Texas warehouse.

u056.text: Its workers can finish ten billion operations in about four millionths of a second.

u057.text: Its memory can deliver about eight terabytes a second, which sounds enormous.

u058.text: But watch the race. At that speed, the five gigabyte delivery takes more than six hundred millionths of a second.

u059.text: The truck takes over a hundred times longer than the work.

u060.text: So when the chip writes for just you, its workers sit idle more than ninety nine percent of the time.

u061.text: That is the pause you see. Engineers call it being memory bound.

u062.text: And none of this surprised the people who saw it coming.

u063.text: In nineteen ninety four, two computer scientists at the University of Virginia, William Wulf and Sally McKee, wrote a short paper with a blunt title.

u065.text: Processors were getting faster much more quickly than memory, they pointed out, and the gap kept widening.

u066.text: Sooner or later, they warned, every program would end up waiting for memory instead of computing. Cat's climb is exactly that case.

u067.text: They were right, and the wall is not just about time. It is about energy.

u068.text: Twenty years later, the Stanford engineer Mark Horowitz put numbers on it.

u069.text: Fetching a number from a memory chip cost about a hundred and seventy times more energy than multiplying two numbers.

u070.text: The distance is the cost. Every bit has to be pushed down a wire, and the longer the wire, the more it burns.

u071.text: So the question for everyone building these machines became: how do you stop moving so much?

u072.text: The first answer was to move the warehouse.

u073.text: At AMD, a team led by Bryan Black had been working on it since two thousand eight.

u074.text: Their problem was graphics memory. Its power use simply would not scale to what the next chips needed.

u075.text: So instead of spreading memory chips around the board, they stacked them into towers.

u076.text: Tiny wires run straight down through the silicon, connecting every floor of the tower at once.

u077.text: Then they set the towers right beside the processor, on the same slab of silicon.

u078.text: In June twenty fifteen, AMD's Fiji was the first graphics chip to ship with this stacked memory.

u079.text: Today it is called high bandwidth memory, and every Blackwell chip carries its own towers of it.

u080.text: The road from warehouse to factory is now as short as anyone can make it.

u081.text: But there is a catch. Even on that short road, the truck still takes hundreds of times longer than the work.

u082.text: So the second answer was to stop sending the truck for just one person.

u083.text: Every conversation uses exactly the same weights.

u084.text: So the system gathers many conversations together, and a single delivery carries cat along with everyone else's words.

u085.text: The workers who would nap for you stay busy for a crowd. This is called batching.

u086.text: Except batching has a problem of its own. Every conversation needs a scratchpad.

u087.text: For every word you send or receive, the model keeps the notes it made during attention, so it never has to redo them.

u088.text: Those notes grow with every word and every person, and they fill the memory up.

u089.text: In twenty twenty three, Woosuk Kwon and his colleagues at Berkeley measured how badly.

u090.text: In the serving systems of the time, as little as a fifth of that scratchpad memory held actual notes.

u091.text: The rest was reserved just in case, or lost in gaps between conversations.

u092.text: Their fix came from an old idea in operating systems. Cut memory into small pages and hand them out only when needed.

u093.text: With almost nothing wasted, the same chips could handle two to four times as many requests.

u094.text: A year earlier, Tri Dao and his colleagues had applied the same lesson inside attention itself.

u095.text: Their method, called FlashAttention, keeps the work in a tiny fast memory on the chip, so less has to travel back and forth.

u096.text: The third answer was to make the cargo lighter.

u097.text: In that open model, most weights are stored in just over four bits each, instead of the usual sixteen.

u098.text: Smaller numbers mean a lighter truck on every trip, and the whole model fits on a single chip.

u099.text: But the biggest models do not fit on one chip, and a busy service needs thousands of them.

u100.text: So the chips are wired together, and here the fight against distance gets physical.

u101.text: This is NVIDIA's rack for Blackwell, a cabinet taller than a person that weighs more than a tonne.

u102.text: It holds seventy two of those chips, along with thirty six Grace processors to manage them.

u103.text: Behind them runs a spine of copper cables, more than three kilometres of it, linking every chip to every other.

u104.text: NVIDIA says the rack acts like a single, massive GPU.

u105.text: A model can be cut into slices and spread across it, so each chip only fetches its own slice of cat's climb.

u106.text: Where does all that effort go in the end?

u107.text: It turns into heat. One of these racks draws about a hundred and twenty kilowatts, about as much as a hundred American homes.

u108.text: Air cannot carry that away, so liquid runs through metal plates pressed onto every chip.

u109.text: The heat has to go somewhere, and many sites dump it into the sky through cooling towers.

u110.text: A tower lets a small part of the water evaporate, and the evaporation pulls heat out of the rest.

u111.text: That is where the water in the headlines goes.

u112.text: Days after ChatGPT launched, its chief executive Sam Altman wrote that the compute costs were eye-watering.

u113.text: How much does cat's trip actually cost, then?

u114.text: In twenty twenty five, he put an average query at about a third of a watt hour, about what an oven uses in a second or so.

u115.text: Tiny, for one question. But ChatGPT gets around two and a half billion prompts a day.

u116.text: Together, that is a steady load of about thirty five megawatts, the power of roughly thirty thousand homes.

u117.text: And yet that is a single service, in an industry that is still building.

u118.text: Which brings us back to cat.

u119.text: Light carried it through glass, a trick from a jet of water in eighteen forty two.

u120.text: A file compression idea from a nineteen ninety four magazine turned it into a number.

u121.text: It climbed a tower of weights that had to be trucked in, again and again, for every piece of the answer.

u122.text: Stacked memory shortened the road, batching shared the truck, and smaller numbers lightened the load.

u123.text: Every one of those inventions fights the same wall that two scientists described in nineteen ninety four.

u124.text: Moving a number costs more than using it.

u125.text: So the next time an answer appears a few words at a time, watch the rhythm.

u126.text: That little stutter is not the machine thinking.

u127.text: It is the machine waiting for the truck.
